claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc is composed of two epithelial cell layers: the peripodial epithelium and the disc proper, along with muscle precursors.
source: This larval primordium is composed of two epithelial cell layers, the peripodial epithelium and the disc proper, along with muscle precursors (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the composition of the wing imaginal disc structure.

claim: Damaged wing discs can trigger wound-response mechanisms allowing for disc repair and the formation of normal wings.
source: Damaged wing discs can trigger a set of wound-response mechanisms allowing for disc repair and the formation of normal wings (Smith-Bolton, 2016; Tripathi and Irvine, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: JNK and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are key drivers for the regenerative process in wing discs.
source: The molecular pathways identified as key drivers for this regenerative process include the regulation of cell apoptosis (JNK, JAK/STAT; La Fortezza et al., 2016), cell proliferation (EGFR, Wnt, Wingless, Scalloped; Blanco et al., 2010; Herrera et al., 2013; Irvine and Harvey, 2015; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2015), re-epithelialization (ERK, Grainy head; Mace et al., 2005), and developmental timing (insulin-like peptide 8; Katsuyama et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The multiome dataset yielded 17,402 high-quality cells with a median of 1124 detected genes per cell and a median of 3060 unique ATAC fragments per cell.
source: This yielded 17,402 high-quality cells, with a median of 1124 detected genes per cell, and a median of 3060 unique ATAC fragments per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the multiome experiments.

claim: The integrated wing atlas contains 70,230 cells from 10X Genomics across 10 replicates.
source: The integrated atlas contains 70,230 cells from 10X Genomics, across 10 replicates (four from this work, four from Everetts et al., 2021, one from Bageritz et al., 2019, and one from Deng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the integrated dataset.

claim: One cluster was enriched for cells from wounded disc samples with markers linked to stress response pathways.
source: One cluster was noticeably enriched for cells from the wounded disc samples, with markers linked to stress response pathways (e.g. kayak, insulin-like peptide 8, unpaired3, p-adj <10e–3, log2FC >1.7; Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d) and localized at the wound site in the pouch domain (Figure 1d), suggesting that this cluster represents a wound-response cell state.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data and immunostaining localization.

claim: The wound cluster can be subdivided into two distinct cell populations: population α of 1211 cells and population β of 94 cells.
source: This cluster can furthermore be subdivided at higher resolution into two distinct cell populations (population α of 1211 cells and population β of 94 cells, Figure 1b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of the single-cell data.

claim: Marker genes of late developmental time points are globally downregulated in wounded disc samples.
source: By comparing the up and downregulated genes with respect to the developmental time, we found that marker genes of late time points (e.g. ecdysone-inducible gene E2) are globally downregulated in the wounded disc samples dissected at the same time point.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: There is a significant overlap of downregulated markers for both wound response and developmental timing (21%, p-adj <10e–3).
source: We furthermore found a significant overlap of downregulated markers for both wound response and developmental timing (21%, p-adj <10e–3, Fisher's exact test, Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: Wounding triggers a global reaction across the whole disc which delays development to give more time for wound repair before metamorphosis.
source: This resemblance of wounded disc cells with those from earlier stage wild-type larvae confirms that wounding triggers a global reaction across the whole disc which delays development to give more time for the wound to repair completely before metamorphosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of gene expression patterns between wounded and developmental time-course samples.

claim: The developmental delay is likely driven by insulin-like peptide 8 (ilp8), a critical long-range regulator of ecdysone signaling.
source: This delay is likely driven by insulin-like peptide 8 (ilp8), a critical long-range regulator of ecdysone signaling, highly expressed in the wound cluster (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and previous knowledge about ilp8 function.

claim: The eGRN inference approach resulted in 147 high-quality eGRNs spanning 98 TFs, with on average 54 target genes and 58 target regions.
source: This procedure resulted in 147 high-quality eGRNs (85 activating, 62 repressing), spanning 98 TFs, with on average 54 target genes and 58 target regions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational analysis results.

claim: The blistered eGRN is specifically active in the pouch domain.
source: In the case of bs, we found the eGRN to be specifically active in the pouch, both from the gene expression and the region accessibility perspectives (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN activity scoring from both RNA and ATAC data.

claim: The Sox15 eGRN is one of the strongest regulatory programs observed in the hinge.
source: One of the strongest regulatory programs was observed in the hinge with the Sox box protein 15 (Sox15) (Dichtel-Danjoy et al., 2009) eGRN (22 genes, 36 regions, Figure 2c and d) where the top predicted target genes included zn finger homeodomain 2, frizzled, dachsous, and homothorax.
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN analysis and regulon specificity scoring.

claim: Both wound clusters α and β are associated with 3980 enhancers, of which 24% have been previously described as damage-responsive regulatory elements.
source: These two clusters are associated to 3980 enhancers (DARs, see 'Materials and methods,' Supplementary file 3), among which 24% have been previously described as damage-responsive regulatory elements (Harris et al., 2020; Vizcaya-Molina et al., 2018), including the BRV118 locus (Gracia-Latorre et al., 2022; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published damage-responsive elements.

claim: The Jra/Kay eGRNs show high and specific activity in the wound populations at both gene expression and chromatin accessibility levels.
source: The activity of the JNK pathway is further confirmed by a high and specific activity of the Jra/Kay eGRNs in the wound populations, at both gene expression and chromatin accessibility levels (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN activity analysis from multiome data.

claim: The eGRN of Stat92E is specifically active in the wound response clusters.
source: We also confirm the strong involvement of JAK/STAT as the eGRN of Signal-transducer and activator of transcription protein at 92E (Stat92E) is specifically active in the wound response clusters (Figure 3a), in agreement with the enrichment for the Stat92E binding motif in the wound-specific accessible regions (NES = 3.6) and the co-expression of the unpaired ligands (upd1/2/3, Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN activity analysis, motif enrichment, and gene expression data.

claim: AP1 is the largest inferred wound eGRN with 470 target genes and 689 target regions.
source: AP1 is the largest inferred wound eGRN (470 target genes, 689 target regions) and its binding motifs (CRE : TRE variants, Fonseca et al., 2019) are strongly enriched in DARs from both wound populations α an β (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN inference results and motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Wound population α shows upregulation of markers of tissue patterning and proliferation relative to population β.
source: We further observe an upregulation of markers of tissue patterning and proliferation in cluster α relative to cluster β, like wingless (wg), Wnt oncogene analog 6 (Wnt6) (Figure 1c, p-adjα/β < 10e–3, log2FCα/β > 1) and CyclinE (CycE) (Figure 3d, log2FCα/β > 0.8).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis between the two wound populations.

claim: There is a significant overlap between wound population α marker genes and genes identified in a study showing JAK/STAT coordinates cell proliferation during wing disc regeneration.
source: Consistent with the higher enhancer activity of the Stat92E eGRN in wound α compared to β (Figure 3a and b), we find a significant overlap between the α marker genes and a study that identified JAK/STAT as coordinating cell proliferation during wing disc regeneration (GSEA, NES = 1.292) (Katsuyama et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing with published data.

claim: Ets21C is upregulated in wound population α with combined enrichment of its gene expression and binding motif.
source: We also find evidence for an upregulation of the pro-regenerative marker Ets at 21C (Ets21C) (Worley et al., 2022), with a combined enrichment of its gene expression (p-adj < 10e–3, log2FC > 8) and an enrichment of the Ets21C binding motif in cluster α (cistarget, NES = 3.35).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis and motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Wound population β shows upregulation of genes associated with innate immunity, glutathione metabolism, cell migration signaling, response to irradiation, and negative regulation of cell cycle.
source: Genes found upregulated in β compared to α include genes associated with innate immunity (Dorsal-related immunity factor), glutathione metabolism (Glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit, Glutathione S transferase D9)(p-adjβ/α<10e–3, log2FCβ/α > 2), cell migration signaling (e.g rho1, slow border and pvf1, p-adj <10e–3), response to irradiation (e.g. inverted repeat-binding protein, p-adj <10e–3) and negative regulation of cell cycle (e.g. growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45, tribbles).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis between wound populations.

claim: Wound population β cells are located at the center of the wounded pouch despite their lack of pouch-specification markers.
source: The cells expressing these markers are located at the center of the wounded pouch, despite their lack of pouch-specification markers (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial localization data from immunostaining.

claim: Wound population β shows similarities with cellular senescence based on markers of stress-response, DNA-damage response, paracrine signaling, and cell cycle stalling.
source: Indeed, a recent study in wounded wing imaginal discs associate the emergence of senescent-like cells with the presence of markers of stress-response (jra, kay), DNA-damage response (gadd45), paracrine signaling (pvf1), and cell cycle stalling (trbl), as observed in our population β (Cosolo et al., 2019; Jaiswal et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published senescence markers.

claim: The TFs irbp18, xrp1, slbo, vri, and sox14 have strong specificity scores for the senescent population β.
source: By examining eGRN activities, we find several TFs with a strong specificity score for the senescent population (β), namely the heterodimer partners inverted repeat binding protein 18 kDa (irbp18) and xrp1, slbo, vrille (vri), and sox box protein 14 (sox14) (top 6% RSS, Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by regulon specificity score analysis.

claim: The bZip TFs irbp18 and vri are significantly upregulated in the senescent population compared to the proliferative population.
source: Among them, the two bZip TFs irbp18 and vri are significantly upregulated in the senescent population compared to the proliferative population (α) (p-adj <2 * 10e–3, log2FCβ/α>2.4) and share similarities in their TF binding motifs with the mammalian, senescence-associated C/EBP proteins (Figure 3b; Blanco et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and motif similarity comparison.

claim: The Irbp18 eGRN is composed of 149 predicted target regions and 116 target genes.
source: The Irbp18 eGRN (extended category, see method) is composed of 149 predicted target regions (80 wound-specific and 11 senescent-specific regions) and 116 target genes (52 markers of senescent population, p-adj <5 * 10e–3, log2FC > 1.5) including slbo, vri, ets at 98B (ets98B), socs36E, head involution defective (hid), growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45 (gadd45) and p53.
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN inference results.

claim: There is significant enrichment for C/EBPB-like binding motifs in senescent-specific peaks (NES = 5.25).
source: The presence of these TFs in the senescent cluster (β) is further corroborated by the significant enrichment for C/EBPB-like binding motifs in senescent-specific peaks (NES = 5.25, Figure 3b and c) generated using MACS2 bdgdiff (Zhang et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis on differential peaks.

claim: There is significant enrichment for the Scalloped motif in senescent-specific accessible regions (NES = 4.89).
source: Despite the absence of Sd mRNA upregulation, nuclear Sd protein may increase in the senescent population since we find a significant enrichment for the Sd motif in the senescent-specific accessible regions (NES = 4.89).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The top enriched motif in senescent-specific regions is a C/EBP-TEAD dimer motif (NES = 7.48).
source: In fact, the top enriched motif in these senescent-specific regions is a C/EBP-TEAD dimer motif (NES = 7.48, Figure 3c), notably found in the enhancer of CG13024, a strong marker of both senescent and rasV12 scrib-/- cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, see next section).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: 200 genes were significantly upregulated in response to Xrp1 overexpression (DEseq2, logFC > 1.5, p-adj < 5.10e–3).
source: The 200 significantly upregulated genes (DEseq2, logFC > 1.5, p-adj < 5.10e–3) in response to Xrp1 overexpression were strongly enriched for markers of cellular senescence (Reactome Pathway Database, Gillespie et al., 2022) and α and β wound populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from bulk RNA-seq.

claim: Genes upregulated by Xrp1 overexpression are enriched for inferred target gene sets of C/EBP eGRNs.
source: As an additional validation of our eGRN construction, we also find the inferred target gene sets of C/EBP eGRNs significantly enriched among the upregulated genes (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of Xrp1 overexpression data.

claim: The rasV12scrib-/- signature is enriched for the binding motifs of Stat92E (NES = 4.19) and AP-1 (NES = 7.17).
source: In agreement with Davie et al., 2015 this signature is enriched for the binding motifs of Stat92E (NES = 4.19) and AP-1 (NES = 7.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and comparison with previous study.

claim: There is significant enrichment for the rasV12scrib-/- signature regions in both proliferative (α) and senescent (β) wound populations compared to wild-type pouch cells (p-adj < 10e–3).
source: Looking at pseudo-bulk ATAC aggregate wing disc data, we noted a significant enrichment for the rasV12scrib-/- signature regions for both proliferative (α) and senescent (β) wound populations in contrast to wild-type pouch cells (p-adj < 10e–3, one-tailed t-test, Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The integrated wound and tumor analysis reveals co-clustering of senescent wound cells (β) with rasV12scrib-/- and scrib-/- cells.
source: This analysis reveals a co-clustering of the senescent wound cells (β) with rasV12scrib-/- and scrib-/- cells (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by integrated single-cell clustering analysis.

claim: Both proliferative and senescent signatures are upregulated in oncogenic models, with the strongest increase for the senescent signature.
source: We find both signatures to be upregulated, with the strongest increase in gene expression between wild-type and the two oncogenic models for the senescent signature (p-adj < 10e–3, one-tailed t-test, Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene signature activity.

claim: Four tumor subpopulations were detected in rasV12scrib-/- tumors, delimited by expression gradients of wound β and C/EBP target gene markers.
source: To further explore cellular heterogeneity in rasV12scrib-/- tumors, we performed a sub-clustering analysis and detected four tumor subpopulations, delimited by the expression gradient of several markers of wound β and C/EBP targets genes such as Gadd45 and CG13024 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by sub-clustering analysis of tumor cells.

claim: Two distinct wound populations display proliferative (α) and senescent (β) properties.
source: Using this new eGRN viewpoint, we found two distinct populations respectively displaying proliferative (α) and senescent (β) properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN analysis and marker gene expression patterns.

claim: Both wound populations share a common wound response program comprising JNK and JAK/STAT signaling.
source: Both populations share a common wound response program, comprising JNK and JAK/STAT signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by eGRN activity analysis showing shared activation of these pathways.

claim: Senescent cells display additional activation of DNA damage, paracrine signaling, and stress mitigation pathways distinct from proliferative cells.
source: Yet, the senescent cells display an additional activation of DNA damage, paracrine signaling, and stress mitigation pathways (glutathione metabolism, FCα/β > 1.8) that is distinct from the proliferative cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis between the two wound populations.

claim: TFs associated with pouch fate specification are downregulated in senescent cells.
source: In agreement with a possible de-differentiation process, TFs associated with pouch fate specification are also downregulated in senescent cells (Distal-less, blistered, engrailed).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis and inference about de-differentiation.

claim: Senescence markers co-vary with C/EBP-like eGRN activity and oncogenic signatures.
source: Concurrently, the senescence markers co-vary with C/EBP-like eGRN activity and the oncogenic signatures (rasV12scrib-/- and scrib-/-, top 100 target genes, Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of eGRN activity and gene signatures.

claim: A common response program is shared by all wound populations and rasV12scrib-/- cancer cells (JNK, JAK/STAT).
source: Taken together, these results highlight a common response program, shared by all wound populations and rasV12scrib-/- cancer cells (JNK, JAK/STAT), and an additional senescent-like program driven by C/EBP-like TFs that is shared between the senescent population and the tumorigenesis paradigms.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of eGRN activities across conditions.

claim: This study presents the first depiction of the senescence phenotype at the single cell multiomic level (scRNA+scATAC).
source: To our knowledge, this study presents the first depiction of the senescence phenotype at the single cell multiomic level (scRNA+scATAC).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the novelty of their approach.

claim: Tumor programs are highly similar to the senescent-like cell population emerging following a transient wound.
source: In this study, we found tumor programs to be highly similar to the senescent-like cell population emerging following a transient wound.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of gene expression and chromatin accessibility patterns.

claim: A tumor paradigm can be seen as a wound that never heals, where failure to arrest cell proliferation prevents damaged cells from fully resorbing.
source: From this perspective, we can see a tumor paradigm as a wound that never heals, where the failure to arrest cell proliferation would prevent the damaged cells to fully resorb.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual interpretation based on the observed similarities between wound and tumor responses.

claim: Senescent cells lead collective migration of proliferative cells toward wound closure and are then discarded through mechanical competition.
source: Recent studies further suggest a guiding role, where senescent cells lead the collective migration of proliferative cells toward wound closure, where they are then discarded through mechanical competition (Álvarez-Fernández et al., 2015; Kozyrska et al., 2022; Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Failure to arrest SASP signaling through senescent cell clearance would promote overproliferation in persistent oncogenic induction.
source: Following this hypothesis, failure to arrest SASP signaling through senescent cell clearance would promote overproliferation in persistent oncogenic induction.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Polarity sensing mutants (e.g. scrib-/-) overproliferate when present as a homogeneous population but are cleared within a crowd of wild-type cells.
source: This idea of competition-mediated clearance is supported by several studies showing that polarity sensing mutants (e.g. scrib-/-) would overproliferate when present as a homogeneous population, but would be cleared within a crowd of wild-type cells (Ballesteros-Arias et al., 2014; Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Pinal et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA damage-responsive TF p53 and cell cycle stalling cooperate to trigger cellular senescence.
source: Previously it was shown that the DNA damage-responsive TF p53 and cell cycle stalling cooperate to trigger cellular senescence (Kozyrska et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cell cycle stalling in the Drosophila wound model is mediated by AP-1 and involves tribbles.
source: Such stalling has also been reported in the Drosophila wound model, where it is mediated by AP-1 and involves tribbles (Cosolo et al., 2019), two markers of our senescent population.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study and correlation with markers in the current study.

claim: JNK activity protects damaged, senescent cells from competition as long as they do not resume cycling.
source: The authors further highlight that JNK activity is protecting the damaged, senescent cells from competition as long as they do not resume cycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A positive feedback loop via moladietz sustains JNK activity in senescent cells after wounding.
source: Two other studies have also demonstrated the role of a positive feedback loop via moladietz (marker of our proliferative population α) to sustain JNK activity in the senescent cells after wounding (Khan et al., 2017; Pinal et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific expression of retrotransposons TAHRE and Invader4 is found in wound populations (p-adj < 10e–3, log2FC > 1).
source: In line with this hypothesis, we find specific expression of the retrotransposons TAHRE and Invader4 in the wound populations (p-adj < 10e–3, log2FC > 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), although further investigation would be necessary to fully characterize this TE-mediated response.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis of transposable elements.

claim: The Hippo pathway is not detected as a wound signature in the rn-egr model, although enrichment of its effector's motif, Scalloped, is found in the senescent wound population.
source: The Hippo pathway (pro-proliferative and pro-invasive in rasV12scrib-/-) is also not detected as a wound signature in our rn-egr model, although we find an enrichment of its effector's motif, Scalloped, in the senescent wound population.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and absence of gene expression changes.

claim: The presence of Scalloped is consistent with reported cooperation of its human ortholog, TEAD, with AP-1 in invasive mesenchymal-like cells.
source: The presence of sd is consistent with the reported cooperation of its human ortholog, TEAD, with AP-1 in invasive mesenchymal-like cells (Verfaillie et al., 2015; Zanconato et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing TEAD-AP1 cooperation.

claim: Senescent cells are capable of surviving apoptotic signals by cell-cycle stalling and guide migration and growth of the pro-regenerative population via strong secretory phenotype.
source: Our data supports a model in which these senescent cells are capable of surviving apoptotic signals by cell-cycle stalling, and then further guide the migration and growth of the pro-regenerative population (α) via its strong secretory phenotype, notably targets of the JNK pathway (i.e. presence of Wg and Upd family ligands; La Marca and Richardson, 2020).
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the observed data and previous knowledge.

claim: The significant similarity between senescent cells and rasV12scrib-/- cells suggests they share the same regulatory wound programs.
source: The significant similarity between senescent cells and rasV12scrib-/- cells suggests that they share the same regulatory wound programs, highlighting the fact that mechanisms present in oncogenic induction may already be active in a genetically wild-type context.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the comparative analysis of gene expression and chromatin accessibility.

claim: A recent study observed different spatial patterns of markers at the wound site in the rasV12scrib-/- model arising from persistent JNK/STAT regulatory network activity.
source: A recent study from Jaiswal et al., 2022 observed different spatial patterns of markers at the wound site in the rasV12scrib-/- model. These populations arise after a persistent activity of a JNK/STAT regulatory network that stratifies signaling activity and cell behavior around the wound site, analogous to morphogen gradient fields in development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Multiple bZip TFs present in this study are conserved in mammalian inflammatory pathways and are capable of forming heterodimers.
source: Regarding TF cooperation events, multiple bZip TFs present in our study are conserved in the mammalian inflammatory pathways and are capable of forming heterodimers (Blanco et al., 2020; Deppmann et al., 2006; Deppmann et al., 2006; Huggins et al., 2015; Newton and Dixit, 2012; Shokri et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on TF conservation and dimerization.

claim: A recent study in YAP/TAZ-bound regions upregulated in breast cancer detected increased binding co-occurrence for orthologs of key regulatory TFs: AP-1, STAT3, C/EBP, and TEAD.
source: Notably, a recent study in YAP/TAZ-bound regions upregulated in breast cancer has detected an increased binding co-occurrence for the orthologs of our key regulatory TFs: AP-1, STAT3, C/EBP, and TEAD (Jra, kay, Stat92E, Sd, Irbp18, slbo) (He et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study in mammalian cancer.
